repos.title: When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
repos.paper_summary: This paper analyzes marginal utility in LLM test-time compute scaling, identifying that extended reasoning often degrades performance through "overthinking." The authors define a flip ratio to track when models abandon correct answers for incorrect ones as token budgets increase. Using DeepSeek-R1-32B and s1-32B on AIME 2024/2025, MATH-500, and GPQA Diamond, they measure accuracy across reasoning budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens via budget forcing. Results show marginal utility turns negative beyond 12K tokens, with the flip ratio exceeding 1.0 at approximately 7K tokens, indicating net harm from additional thinking. Easy problems (Level 1–2) exhibit overthinking at 2K tokens, while hard problems benefit up to 8K. A cost-aware evaluation framework using a tunable $\lambda$ parameter demonstrates that stopping at moderate budgets reduces computation by 50% with only 6% accuracy loss compared to peak performance. Limitations include the focus on mathematical and scientific reasoning tasks and the use of forced continuations, though natural long-reasoning samples confirm similar degradation patterns.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper tests whether more reasoning tokens keep improving accuracy and tracks answers that flip from correct to incorrect.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work reports accuracy gains with compute, and some concurrent studies document overthinking, but few measure marginal returns.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Compute is measured in reasoning tokens, using budget forcing, with marginal utility, flip events, and overthinking indicators defined.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Two 32B models show accuracy peaking near 12K tokens and flip ratios above 1 from about 7K tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Cost-Aware Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Cost-weighted scoring favors stopping near 6K tokens, which yields about 50% compute reduction for about 6% accuracy loss.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Marginal utility falls at high budgets and models overthink, so the authors urge reporting efficiency frontiers alongside accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover only math and science tasks and open-weight models, and causal mechanisms of overthinking remain untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The authors argue that identifying wasted extra computation can reduce energy use and emissions from language model inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers how natural long-reasoning samples were selected, their accuracy by output length, and their reconsideration patterns.

repos.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
repos.paper_summary:
Mamba is a sequence model architecture that replaces Transformer attention with selective state space models (SSMs) to achieve linear-time scaling. The method makes SSM parameters $\Delta$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ functions of the input, allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information based on content. Because this input-dependency prevents standard convolutional computation, the authors implement a hardware-aware parallel scan algorithm that performs discretization and recurrence in GPU SRAM rather than HBM, using recomputation during backpropagation to limit memory usage.

The architecture combines the SSM layer and MLP into a single block without attention. On language modeling tasks, Mamba-3B outperforms Pythia-3B by 4 points on average common sense reasoning and matches the performance of Pythia-7B. It achieves 5x higher generation throughput than comparable Transformers. For audio and genomics, Mamba reduces FID scores by more than half compared to baselines like Hyena and SaShiMi. The paper notes that evaluation was limited to models below 7B parameters and that the selection mechanism may reduce performance on continuous data modalities where linear time-invariant SSMs excel.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Transformers are costly on long sequences, and Mamba adds input-dependent state space dynamics that scale linearly and match Transformers on language.

digest_headlines.heading: State Space Models
digest_headlines.headline: Structured state space models are linear time-invariant, so their parameters stay fixed across time steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Selective State Space Models
digest_headlines.headline: Selection lets SSM parameters depend on the input, which breaks convolution, so a hardware-aware scan computes the model efficiently.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show Mamba solves synthetic recall tasks and outperforms baselines on language, DNA and audio, with 5× higher throughput.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Selective SSMs trade off on continuous data such as audio, and scaling beyond small sizes remains unassessed.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Mamba is a strong candidate for a general sequence backbone, with selection giving context-dependent reasoning at linear scaling in length.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers selection versus gating, related work, speech-generation training details, and efficiency benchmarks.

repos.title: OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents
repos.paper_summary: OpenHands is an open-source platform for building and evaluating AI agents that act on the world by writing code, running shell commands, and browsing the web. Its main components are an event stream that records actions and observations, a Docker-sandboxed runtime with a bash shell, an IPython server, and a Chromium browser, an AgentSkills library of editing and document-parsing tools, and an AgentHub of community agents, including the default CodeAct agent. Agents can delegate subtasks to other agents, and users can add agents or new Docker images. The evaluation framework covers 15 benchmarks, including SWE-Bench, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, and WebArena. The paper reports results across these tasks, but the text provided here does not include the per-benchmark scores, so this summary cannot state them. The platform is released under the MIT license and has 32K GitHub stars and more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors. The paper acknowledges that building agents that are safe and reliable remains an open challenge, which its appendix covers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: OpenHands is a community platform for building agents that write code, use a shell, and browse the web.

digest_headlines.heading: OpenHands Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Agents are defined by a step function over an event stream, and actions run in a Docker sandbox that returns observations.

digest_headlines.heading: AgentHub: A Hub of Community-Contributed Agents
digest_headlines.headline: The AgentHub ships a default CodeAct agent, a browsing agent, a graph-based agent, and a template for micro agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Across 15 benchmarks, the CodeActAgent resolves 26% of software engineering issues and fixes 79.3% of Python bugs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: OpenHands is presented as a community platform that accelerates research and applications of agentic AI systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers limitations, ethics, related work, the graphical interface, integration tests, runtime image building, graduate-level benchmark results, prompts, skills, and BrowserGym actions.

repos.title: AgentScope: A Flexible yet Robust Multi-Agent Platform
repos.paper_summary: AgentScope is a Python-based multi-agent platform that uses message exchange as its core communication mechanism. It provides pipelines and a message hub to structure agent workflows, along with pre-built agents for dialogue, code execution, and image generation. The system handles fault tolerance through service-level retries, rule-based format correction, and customizable handlers for model-resolvable errors. For distributed deployment, an actor-based framework allows developers to use identical workflow code for both local and remote execution without modifying the application logic. Multi-modal data is transmitted via URLs in messages, employing lazy loading to reduce bandwidth overhead during inter-agent communication. A drag-and-drop workstation generates JSON configurations or Python scripts from visual DAGs, enabling non-programmers to build applications. Tool usage follows a ReAct pattern where a service toolkit manages function registration, prompt engineering, and response parsing. The paper does not provide quantitative benchmarks comparing AgentScope against other frameworks like AutoGen or LangChain; instead, it documents architectural features and API interfaces. Limitations include the reliance on LLM capabilities for semantic error detection and the requirement for human intervention when unresolvable errors, such as expired API keys, occur.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent application development is hard, so the paper proposes AgentScope, a platform built around message exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Overview
digest_headlines.headline: AgentScope defines four core concepts (message, agent, service, workflow) and a three-layer architecture.

digest_headlines.heading: High Usability
digest_headlines.headline: Pipelines, a message hub, built-in agents, and a drag-and-drop workstation are offered to reduce development effort.

digest_headlines.heading: Fault-Tolerant Mechanisms
digest_headlines.headline: Errors are sorted into four levels, each handled by retries, rule-based correction, customizable handlers, or logging.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Modal Applications
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-modal data is passed as URLs in messages, with files loaded only when needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Tool Usage
digest_headlines.headline: The service toolkit implements a ReAct loop with four steps: function preparation, instructions, reasoning, and acting.

digest_headlines.heading: Agents with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: Retrieval-augmented generation support uses a one-file configuration and shared knowledge banks that agents can update and weight.

digest_headlines.heading: Actor-based Distributed Framework
digest_headlines.headline: An actor-based distributed mode lets the same workflow run locally or across machines, using placeholder messages.

digest_headlines.heading: Signature Applications of AgentScope
digest_headlines.headline: Example applications include basic and group conversation, a six-player werewolf game, a retrieval-augmented generation copilot, web search, and a database query agent.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Related frameworks such as LangChain, AutoGen, MetaGPT, and ChatDev are grouped into language agent and multi-agent frameworks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that AgentScope lowers barriers to multi-agent development and lists RAG and adaptive protocols as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix points to a GitHub repository and lists example dialogue histories for standalone conversation and werewolf.

repos.title: Spatial Metaphors for LLM Memory: A Critical Analysis of the MemPalace Architecture
repos.paper_summary: This preprint analyzes MemPalace, an open-source memory system for LLMs that organizes stored text as Wings, Rooms, and Drawers. It maps each layer to the code and attributes the reported LongMemEval results to individual components. The authors find that the palace hierarchy is a flat ChromaDB collection with metadata filtering. The 96.6% Recall@5 (at least one correct session in the top five) comes from verbatim text embedded with ChromaDB's default all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model, without palace structure. Room-based boosting reaches 89.4%, and the lossy AAAK mode reaches 84.2%. Mem0's April 2026 algorithm reports 93.4%. The paper credits the verbatim-first design, the zero-LLM write path, and a wake-up cost of about 170 tokens. It finds no computational benefit from the spatial metaphor and no implemented contradiction detection. Limitations: the core analysis covers v3.1.0, later releases are discussed separately, benchmark findings rely partly on a third-party audit and maintainer corrections, and the paper is not peer-reviewed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Persistent memory for language models is an open problem, and MemPalace's claimed 96.6% Recall@5 prompted this audit.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The spatial metaphor may help users, the authors argue, but it does not change the underlying vector retrieval.

digest_headlines.heading: System Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: MemPalace's hierarchy is metadata on one flat ChromaDB collection, so wings and rooms act as search filters.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation and Benchmarks
digest_headlines.headline: An independent audit found the 96.6% result reproduces with plain ChromaDB, and six benchmark claims were corrected.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Verbatim storage, zero-LLM writes and low wake-up cost are the main contributions, while metadata filtering and chunking are standard practice.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Systems in Detail
digest_headlines.headline: Every listed competitor calls an LLM at write time, and reported LongMemEval scores vary widely.

digest_headlines.heading: A Framework for Evaluating AI Memory Systems
digest_headlines.headline: A multi-dimensional framework shows MemPalace leads on fidelity, cost and privacy but trails on relational depth and scalability.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: MemPalace is architecturally standard, the authors conclude, yet its verbatim-first insight and zero-cost writes are useful.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists codebase statistics, reproduction conditions, a glossary, and the analysis disclosure for version 3.1.0.

repos.title: Möbius: A Unified Motion-Language Model Bridging Understanding and Generation
repos.paper_summary: Möbius is a unified motion-language model that runs the full motion diffusion process inside the same multimodal attention space as text and motion understanding, rather than conditioning an external diffusion module on language-model features. It operates on continuous frame-level raw motion (D=201) with no discrete tokenizer or pretrained motion VAE. Training is two-stage: motion captioning first, then generation with the understanding parameters frozen. On HumanML3D text-to-motion, Möbius-0.6B reports R@1 0.821 and FID 6.13, versus 0.671 and 21.0 for MotionGPT3, the strongest unified baseline in Table 1. The 1.7B variant, trained on 1,700 hours of motion data, reports FID 10.7. Motion captioning (Table 2) reports BLEU-4 0.203 for the 0.6B model against 0.161 for MotionGPT3. On MotionFix editing, the 0.6B variant with additional MotionFix data reports FID 0.0955 against 0.134 for MotionLab. Limitations stated by the authors: experiments cover only controlled single-person motion, with multi-person interaction, detailed hand motion, and retargeting left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius runs the entire motion diffusion process inside the shared multimodal space used for understanding, not an external module.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior unified motion models either tokenize motion or hand language features to an external diffusion module.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius uses raw frame-level motion with role-specific parameters and shared attention, trained understanding-first.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius-0.6B scores 0.8209 on top-1 retrieval and 6.1291 on Fréchet distance, ahead of unified baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the shared space works at 1.7B scale, with evidence limited to controlled single-person motion.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists datasets, architecture and training settings, task construction, inference settings, timing, evaluation protocols, and extra completion results.

repos.title: Codebase-Memory: Tree-Sitter-Based Knowledge Graphs for LLM Code Exploration via MCP
repos.paper_summary:
Codebase-Memory is an open-source system that constructs a Tree-Sitter-based knowledge graph to expose structural code queries to LLM agents via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The pipeline parses 66 languages, resolves calls using a six-strategy cascade, and detects communities with the Louvain algorithm. It stores the resulting graph in SQLite and exposes 14 typed query tools through a single statically linked C binary with zero runtime dependencies.

Evaluated across 31 real-world repositories, the MCP Agent achieved an 83% answer quality score compared to 92% for a file-exploration agent, while consuming ten times fewer tokens ($\sim$1,000 vs. $\sim$10,000) and requiring 2.1 times fewer tool calls. Query latency was under 1 ms for the MCP agent versus 10–30 s for the explorer. Limitations include reduced accuracy on macro-heavy C code (58% quality) and the absence of source-level context, which requires fallback to file exploration for exhaustive pattern matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Text-based code exploration by coding agents scales poorly, so the paper proposes a queryable code knowledge graph exposed via MCP.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work builds heavyweight code graphs or improves agent strategy, leaving the retrieval layer largely unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: Codebase-Memory parses 66 languages into one SQLite knowledge graph and serves it through 14 MCP tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On 31 languages the MCP agent scored 0.83 against 0.92 for the explorer while using 2.1 times fewer tool calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Structure helps cross-file queries, but results come from one backend and one repository per language.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues structural retrieval is a viable foundation for LLM-based code intelligence.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Availability Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, benchmark scripts and evaluation data are public for the evaluated release v0.5.5.

repos.title: Solv3R: 3D Looped Transformer as a Multi-view Solver
repos.paper_summary:
Solv3R reformulates multi-view 3D reconstruction as a stationary looped transformer solver: one shared update operator is applied at every call, independent of how many calls a view has already received. It is fine-tuned from the pretrained DéjàView model, with learned constant gates replacing iteration-conditioned gates and the state rescaled to a fixed RMS norm after each update. Training uses random gradient-free solver calls, differentiable calls supervised after 24 to 48 calls, Gaussian noise or partial resets, and distillation of DéjàView outputs after 16 calls.

On the offline benchmarks in Table 1 (DTU, ETH3D, 7-Scenes, ScanNet++, nuScenes), Solv3R with 16 fixed calls reaches camera AUC@30 of 99.0 on DTU and 94.8 on ETH3D, close to DéjàView's 98.8 and 95.4. Adaptive stopping, which halts when the relative state update falls below γ = 0.02, uses 91.3 TFLOPs for 24 views, versus 75.9 for DéjàView at 16 calls. Under perturbation, Solv3R recovers accurate poses where DéjàView does not.

Limitations: the stability and correction results come from selected windows, and the stopping rule's reliability on other datasets appears only in the supplement. Solv3R's behavior beyond 64 calls is not reported in the main text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Feed-forward geometric models struggle to refine or extend reconstructions, so the paper proposes Solv3R, a reusable learned solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans feed-forward geometry, looped refinement and streaming reconstruction, which Solv3R applies as one solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A stationary learned update, trained for stability, correction and continuation, is shared across all solver calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Solver analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Solv3R's camera error stays low as updates shrink and recovers after perturbation, unlike DéjàView.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Solv3R's accuracy at 16 calls is comparable to DéjàView, and it is competitive across offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues that a single learned solver can unify offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming reconstruction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, evaluation protocols, extra analyses, a failure case and additional aerial and qualitative results.

repos.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
repos.paper_summary: VisSearch-Bench is a benchmark of 204 human-written tasks for evaluating visual context management in long-horizon open-web search by multimodal agents. The tasks span five categories: Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide–Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search, across 7 primary and 25 secondary domains. Annotators build each task from public sources with a reference answer and traceable evidence, and automated checks plus human review remove tasks that can be solved without the visual evidence. Accuracy requires the predicted answer to contain all and only the required content. Process Score is the fraction of labeled critical states recovered, averaged over tasks. Across 16 models and agent setups, the best system reaches 26.47% accuracy, a ReAct agent with Kimi-K3. Direct answering by GPT-5.5 scores 6.37%, and ReAct with GPT-5.5 reaches 25.49%. Several open-source models score 0.00% accuracy on the direct setting. The paper states that the benchmark's 204 tasks are a limited sample and that the construction relies on human annotation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Some search tasks use images only to identify an entity, so the paper tests how agents link visual evidence across steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: VisSearch-Bench is the only listed benchmark that covers set answers, evidence links, and partial credit together.

digest_headlines.heading: VisSearch-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each of 204 tasks is built from public sources with traceable evidence, a locked answer, and human review.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Search lifts accuracy well above direct answering, but the best system still fully solves only 26.47% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Verifying multiple objects and combining findings into consistent answers remain open challenges for multimodal search agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related benchmark details, prompts, hyperparameters, release fields, and seventeen case-study trajectories.

repos.title: DocLayNet: A Large Human-Annotated Dataset for Document-Layout Analysis
repos.paper_summary:
DocLayNet is a publicly available dataset of 80,863 human-annotated PDF pages designed for document layout analysis. The annotations consist of labeled bounding boxes across 11 classes (e.g., Text, Table, Formula) in COCO format. Unlike previous datasets derived from scientific repositories, DocLayNet includes diverse sources such as financial reports and manuals to capture layout variability. A subset of pages contains double or triple annotations to measure inter-annotator agreement.

Baseline experiments using Mask R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, and YOLOv5 show that model performance lags behind human annotation by approximately 10% in mAP@0.5–0.95. Specifically, the best-performing YOLOv5x6 achieves an overall mAP of 76.8%, compared to the human agreement range of 82–83%. A data ablation study indicates that model accuracy plateaus at 80% of the dataset size. Additionally, splitting data on document boundaries rather than individual pages reduces mAP by roughly 10 points, highlighting the risk of overestimation with page-wise splits. Models trained on DocLayNet demonstrate more consistent cross-dataset performance than those trained on PubLayNet or DocBank.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing layout datasets come from scientific repositories, so DocLayNet adds human-annotated pages with wider layout variety.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior layout analysis moved from rule-based methods to object detection, and newer text-plus-image models lack a shared data format.

digest_headlines.heading: The DocLayNet Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet contains 80863 pages from six document categories, with 11 labels and pre-defined splits that keep documents whole.

digest_headlines.heading: Annotation Campaign
digest_headlines.headline: Four-phase human annotation under a guideline over 100 pages long improved consistency, though 8 of 40 annotators did not pass.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Baseline detectors trail human agreement by 6 to 10%, and random page-wise splits inflate scores by about 10%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet supplies human reference metrics and models that transfer better across datasets, yet a gap to humans remains.
